title: The God who sees (Genesis 16)
hookLine: Hagar, a runaway slave, gives God a name

cards: Abram and Sarai have lived ten years in Canaan, still with no child, and Sarai has stopped waiting.
She takes matters into her own hands: she gives her Egyptian slave, a young woman named Hagar, to Abram, so a child can be born on her behalf. Hagar conceives. And the household cracks.
Hagar looks down on Sarai; Sarai treats her harshly; Abram says, she's your slave, do what you like. So Hagar runs. Pregnant, alone, into the desert, on the road toward Egypt.
Nobody comes after her. Nobody in the camp, anyway.

teach.h: FOUND BY A SPRING, CALLED BY NAME.
teach.b: First, the finding. By a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, the angel of the Lord finds her. In the Douay-Rheims: "Agar, handmaid of Sarai, whence comest thou? and whither goest thou?"
Agar is the old spelling of Hagar. The angel calls her by name. In this chapter, Abram and Sarai never once say her name; she's my handmaid, your handmaid.
And the angel asks her questions, as if her answer matters. Second, the hard part. The angel tells her to go back and submit to Sarai.

teach.h: GO BACK: THE TEXT DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.
teach.b: The text doesn't soften that, and i won't either.
But with it comes a promise: her descendants will be too many to count, and her son will be named Ishmael, which means God hears, because the Lord has heard her affliction. Third, the name.
Then Hagar does something remarkable: she gives God a name. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou the God who hast seen me."
In Hebrew, El Roi, the God who sees. Not Abram. Not a priest.
An Egyptian slave woman, pregnant, on the run, by a well in the desert.

teach.h: THOU THE GOD WHO HAST SEEN ME.
teach.b: The well itself is named after it. Fourth, why it lasts. Catholic social teaching speaks of a God who hears the cry of the poor and sees the overlooked.
Readers find that God here, by a spring in the desert. The person with the least power in the camp is the one who says who God is to her.

how: Catholic social teaching speaks of God hearing the cry of the poor and of a special care for those pushed to the margins.

o: Sarai's name for the angel at the spring
the town in Egypt where Hagar was born

games.q: what's inside Hagar's story — tap the pairs.

s: Hagar gives God a name in Genesis 16
"Thou the God who hast seen me." El Roi.
Abram and Sarai call Hagar by her name
in this story they only call her the slave. the angel is the one who says her name.
the angel tells Hagar she's free to go to Egypt
the angel tells her to go back, a hard word the text doesn't soften, along with a promise.

games.q: you're Hagar, pregnant and alone by a spring in the desert. a messenger of the Lord has called you by name and promised you a son. what do you do?
o: give God a name: the God who sees me.
ask the messenger to bring Sarai.
games.why: she names God: "Thou the God who hast seen me." the well is named after it too.

practice: Think back through yesterday for someone who was there but you didn't really see: the cashier, the cleaner leaving as you arrived, the kid at the edge of the playground, the relative nobody asks a question at dinner.
Say their name to yourself if you know it, and if you don't, notice that. If you pray, hold them before the God who sees.

wordCard.voice: El Roi, the God who sees: the name Hagar, a runaway slave in the desert, gives to God by a spring. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: El Roi, God of seeing, the God who sees me. Hagar's name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: thou god who seest me. The one nobody looked at was seen. Until tomorrow.
